title: No hiding place (123–128)
hookLine: poison can't harm a hand without a wound; not in the sky, the sea or a mountain cave is there escape from one's deeds

lines: THE SKY, THE SEA, A CAVE.
cards: Everybody has a drawer. Maybe a real one, stuffed with the letter you never answered. Maybe a folder on your phone, or a conversation you've steered around for years.
And there's a hope that goes with it: if I move far enough away, change jobs, start fresh somewhere nobody knows me, it won't follow. Sometimes a new start really helps.
But there's one thing a moving truck can't leave behind, and the Dhammapada names it with three places people run to: the sky, the sea and a mountain cave.

teach.b: Chapter nine ends with pictures of protection. Verse one twenty-three: a merchant carrying much wealth with few companions avoids a dangerous road, the way someone who loves life avoids poison.

Then a strange, lovely image, verse one twenty-four: "He who has no wound on his hand, may touch poison with his hand; poison does not affect one who has no wound; nor is there evil for one who does not commit evil."
The harm gets in through the wound. Close the wound, and the poison has nowhere to enter.
Verse one twenty-five adds that harm aimed at an innocent person blows back on the one who threw it, "like light dust thrown up against the wind."

teach.h: NOT SKY, NOT SEA, NOT A CAVE.
teach.b: Then the heart of today, verse one twenty-seven: "Not in the sky, not in the midst of the sea, not if we enter into the clefts of the mountains, is there known a spot in the whole world where a man might be freed from an evil deed."
Nobody is hunting you down. In Buddhist teaching, kamma isn't a judge sending out a posse.

teach.h: THE DEED GOES WHERE YOU GO.
teach.b: The deed comes along because you're the one who did it; it goes wherever you go. That can sound grim, but good deeds travel with you just as surely.
Verse one twenty-eight uses the same three places for death: no spot in the world escapes it.
So the chapter doesn't point toward a better hiding place. It points back to the hand and the wound: fewer wounds, less poison, less to hide.

how: Buddhists understand kamma as the natural result of intentional action rather than a punishment handed down, and many practice confessing faults and taking the precepts again as a way of closing the wound rather than hiding it.

o: only grave crimes, like murder and theft
harmful or unskillful action, small or large
a sin against God that needs forgiving

games.q: match each image to its verse.
p: harm blows back on the thrower

s: verse 124 says poison can't harm a hand that has no wound
"poison does not affect one who has no wound."
in Buddhist teaching, kamma is a judge who hunts you down
the deed comes along because you did it; no one is sent after you.
the chapter recommends a better hiding place
it names the sky, the sea and the mountain caves, and says none of them works.

games.q: you've done something you're ashamed of, and you'd like to be free of it. according to verse 127, where can you go?
o: far away, where nobody knows you.
nowhere: the deed comes with you.
games.why: "not in the sky, not in the midst of the sea, not if we enter into the clefts of the mountains." the way out isn't a place; it's fewer wounds.

practice: Let your hands rest open in your lap and look at them; no need to find a wound. Close your eyes and ask, gently: is there something I'd rather hide?

You don't have to open the whole drawer: notice that it's there, and how the body feels, with no scolding, because seeing it is the first step toward closing the wound. Then come back to the breath, with nothing to run from.

wordCard.voice: Papa. Harm, or unskillful action: verse one twenty-seven's teaching that not in the sky, the sea or a mountain cleft is there a spot where one is freed from it.

orig.note: Pali: harmful, unskillful action; chapter nine is the Pāpavagga, the chapter on evil.

carryVoice: Your line: fewer wounds, less poison. The way out isn't a place. That's day one hundred eighty-three.
